summary.en: Build queries with selection, projection, joins, sets and division, then compare their SQL.
summary.bn: সিলেকশন, প্রজেকশন, জয়েন, সেট ও ডিভিশন দিয়ে কোয়েরি গড়ো এবং এসকিউএলের সঙ্গে মেলাও।

notes: CHECK constraints are enforced from MySQL 8.0.16. The examples also run on MySQL 8.4.

sections.title: Build a question from smaller operations
Match algebra to actual SQL answers
Check the meaning after every operation

examples.title: Selection and projection
examples.explanationHtml: σ first keeps CSE students with known towns. π then keeps the hometown attribute; DISTINCT removes the repeated Dhaka value.

examples.title: Union, intersection and difference
examples.explanationHtml: The union lists 101, 102, 103 and 106. The intersection is 101 and 102; the lab-only difference is 103. EXISTS workarounds also work before MySQL 8.0.31.

examples.title: Cartesian product with renamed attributes
examples.explanationHtml: Two students and two courses create four pairs. The aliases correspond to rename, ρ, and remove ambiguity.

examples.title: Theta join and equality join
examples.explanationHtml: The join condition combines equality on identity with a mark comparison. Three result rows satisfy it.

examples.title: Natural join on deliberately matching names
examples.explanationHtml: Only student_id and section_id share names in these two tables. Both become matching columns; careless natural joins can add unintended conditions.

examples.title: Outer join keeps a missing result
examples.explanationHtml: Student 105 has 55 marks. Student 107 still appears, with NULL, because the left join preserves their enrollment.

examples.title: Division by the required sections
examples.explanationHtml: Students 101 and 102 have both required sections. The two NOT EXISTS clauses mean there is no required section missing for that student.

practice.title: Translate a set difference
practice.statementHtml: Return IDs enrolled in lab section 33 but absent from section 31, ordered by ID. Then test the boundary case of section 36 minus section 31, returning its count as n.
hints: Use an absence test so a matching student is excluded.

practice.title: Check a division with an empty requirement
practice.statementHtml: Return students covering sections 31 and 33, ordered by ID. Then return the count of candidates when the required section set is empty.
hints: An empty required set has no counterexample for any candidate.

practice.title: Translate a phrase in stages
practice.statementHtml: Write algebra for known hometowns of CSE students, without duplicate towns.
practice.answerHtml: πhometown(σdepartment_id=1 ∧ hometown is known(Students)). Start with the student relation. Selection keeps eligible rows; projection removes other attributes and duplicate hometowns. Classical algebra assumes ordinary values, so the known-value condition explicitly excludes SQL NULL here.

practice.title: Reason about join size
practice.statementHtml: Why can joining Students to Results return more rows than there are students?
hints: Count matching pairs, not left rows.
practice.answerHtml: One student may match several results. Ayesha matches three results, so her identifying columns appear three times in the joined rows. The join represents student-result pairs, not one row per student. Project DISTINCT student IDs if the question asks only which students.

practice.title: Explain a theta join
practice.statementHtml: Compare σr.marks ≥ cutoff.minimum(Results × Cutoff) with a theta join.
hints: A theta condition need not be equality.
practice.answerHtml: The product first describes every result-cutoff pair. Selection keeps pairs satisfying the comparison. A theta join expresses that combination directly: Results ⋈marks ≥ minimum Cutoff. The logical answer is the same; the DBMS need not physically create the entire product.

quiz.prompt: Which operation chooses rows satisfying marks ≥ 80?
quiz.explanation: Selection tests a predicate for each tuple; projection chooses columns.

quiz.prompt: What may projection remove in classical algebra?
quiz.explanation: Classical projection returns a set, so equal projected tuples collapse.

quiz.prompt: Why use SELECT DISTINCT for a projection’s SQL equivalent?
options: SQL normally permits duplicate result rows
quiz.explanation: DISTINCT restores set behaviour for the selected columns.

options: When their corresponding attributes have compatible domains
Only when they share a primary key value
quiz.explanation: Union compatibility concerns degree and corresponding domains, not equal row counts.

options: Tuples in R that are absent from S
quiz.explanation: Difference is directional and may change if the operands are swapped.

quiz.prompt: Two rows crossed with three rows produce how many pairs?
quiz.explanation: A Cartesian product pairs every left tuple with every right tuple.

quiz.prompt: Why can NATURAL JOIN change after adding a same-named column?
options: It joins on every shared column name
It always joins only primary keys
quiz.explanation: New shared names add implicit equality conditions.

quiz.prompt: What does relational division express in an enrollment question?
options: Students enrolled in any one section
Students enrolled in every required section
quiz.explanation: Division tests coverage of the whole divisor set, rather than one witness.

quiz.prompt: Which operation keeps unmatched left rows with missing right values?
quiz.explanation: Outer joins extend classical algebra to preserve unmatched rows with NULL-like markers.

quiz.prompt: How many distinct department values remain after projecting Students.department_id?
quiz.code: SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT department_id) AS n FROM students;
quiz.explanation: The projection contains department values 1, 2 and 3.

quiz.prompt: How many pairs are in the full Students × Courses product?
quiz.code: SELECT COUNT(*) AS n FROM students CROSS JOIN courses;
quiz.explanation: Eight students paired with five courses produce forty pairs.

quiz.prompt: How many enrollment tuples survive an inner join to existing results?
quiz.code:
SELECT COUNT(*) AS n FROM enrollments AS e JOIN results AS r
ON e.student_id = r.student_id AND e.section_id = r.section_id;
quiz.explanation: Eleven enrollments have results; the pending one has no matching result tuple.

keyPoints.en: Selection filters tuples while projection chooses attributes.
keyPoints.bn: সিলেকশন সারি বেছে নেয়, প্রজেকশন কলাম বেছে নেয়।

keyPoints.en: Classical relational algebra treats relations as sets.
keyPoints.bn: প্রচলিত রিলেশনাল অ্যালজেব্রায় রিলেশনকে সেট ধরা হয়।

keyPoints.en: Union needs matching attributes and compatible domains.
keyPoints.bn: ইউনিয়নের দুই পাশে মিলযুক্ত অ্যাট্রিবিউট ও ডোমেইন লাগে।

keyPoints.en: A join combines tuples that satisfy its condition.
keyPoints.bn: শর্ত মিলে যাওয়া টিউপলগুলো জয়েনে এক হয়।

keyPoints.en: Division answers questions containing the idea of every.
keyPoints.bn: সবগুলো শর্ত মেটানোর প্রশ্নে ডিভিশন কাজে লাগে।

examQuestions.question: Write algebra for students with marks at least 80, returning unique student IDs.
examQuestions.answerHtml: πstudent_id(σmarks ≥ 80(Results)). Selection keeps three high result tuples. Projection collapses Ayesha’s qualifying repetitions if there are any; the current answer contains 101, 102 and 104. SQL uses DISTINCT student_id with the same mark condition.

examQuestions.question: Explain union, intersection and difference using enrollment sets A={101,102} and B={101,102,103}.
examQuestions.answerHtml: A ∪ B is {101,102,103}. A ∩ B is {101,102}. A − B is empty, while B − A is {103}. The two relations must be union compatible. SQL UNION removes duplicates; EXISTS and NOT EXISTS can express intersection and difference.

examQuestions.question: Explain division and why an empty required-section set needs a policy decision.
examQuestions.answerHtml: Let E(student_id, section_id) represent enrollments and R(section_id) the requirements. Division finds candidates with no missing R value. If R is empty, every candidate passes the universal condition. Decide whether candidates come from all Students or only IDs present in E, because those ranges differ.
